title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
Context: in E420 Euler reformulates the calculus of variations by embedding the sought curve y(x) in a one-parameter family y(x,t). The variation becomes the differential with respect to t, dt(∂y/∂t), and the 'proximal' curves αμ are generated by moving points along a 'generating curve' BN. For J = ∫Z dx with dZ = M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + R dr + ..., where p = y', q = y'', r = y''', integration by parts gives the variation as a sum of 'parts'.

- Part 1: the integral ∫ dt (∂y/∂t)(N − dP/dx + d²Q/dx² − ...) dx. Its vanishing for arbitrary variations gives the Euler–Lagrange (Euler–Poisson) equation.
- Part 2: a boundary term δy·(P − dQ/dx + d²R/dx² − ...).
- Part 3: a boundary term δp·(Q − dR/dx + ...). Here δp = dt (∂²y/∂x∂t) is the change in tangent direction (§44).
- Part 4: a boundary term δq·(R − ...), where δq is the change of curvature.

On this page (end of §45 and §46), Euler concludes as follows.
- The part-3 boundary contribution vanishes if the varied curves have the same tangents as the principal curve at both ends A and M.
- The part-4 contribution vanishes if, in addition, the radii of osculation agree at the ends. Given equal tangents, equal radius of curvature is equivalent to δq = 0.
- Part 2 vanishes if all neighbouring curves pass through both endpoints.
- Part 3 vanishes identically if Z contains no second differentials, since then Q = R = ... = 0. Part 4 vanishes identically unless Z contains third differentials, and so on.
- Together with Part 1 vanishing (the differential equation), this gives the conditions under which the whole first variation vanishes. These are the fixed-endpoint conditions on y, y', y'', ... up to order n−1 for a Lagrangian of order n.

§47 begins the 'Dilucidationes': for ∫Z dx to be extremal, the curve satisfies N − dP/dx + d²Q/dx² − ... = 0. The next page notes that this equation is always of even order (2, 4, 6, ...) unless the coefficients degenerate. It then classifies problems by that order; Class I, where Z = Z(x,y), gives the finite equation N = 0.
errors: No mathematical error. Euler handles only the case where boundary terms are killed by imposing fixed endpoint data (position, tangent, curvature). He does not here derive the natural (transversality) boundary conditions P − dQ/dx + ... = 0 etc. for free ends. That is an omission of scope, not an error.
Minor grammatical slip in the print: 'omnes curuae proximae ... communes habeat tangentes' (should be 'habeant').

ideas.what: Decomposition of the first variation of ∫Z(x,y,y',y'',...)dx into an integral part plus endpoint terms in δy, δy', δy'', ..., each vanishing under fixed endpoint, fixed tangent and fixed curvature conditions
ideas.modern_name: Boundary terms of the first variation for higher-order Lagrangians; essential boundary conditions
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1760-62) for the δ-method boundary terms; Euler E420 and Lagrange's Mécanique analytique
ideas.where_published: E420 (Novi Comm. Acad. Petrop. 16, 1772); also E296 'Elementa calculi variationum'

ideas.what: Variation realised as the derivative with respect to an auxiliary parameter t of a one-parameter family of curves (generating curve BN)
ideas.modern_name: One-parameter family of variations; Gateaux derivative d/dε J(y+εη)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E420), as discussed by C. Fraser in histories of the calculus of variations
ideas.where_published: E420; cf. Opera omnia I.25 introduction (Carathéodory)

ideas.what: The Euler–Lagrange equation for higher-order Lagrangians is always of even order 2n

deep.surprise_reason: Standard, well-documented material from E420 on endpoint terms of the first variation and the fixed-end conditions; it is covered in Carathéodory's Opera omnia introduction and in Fraser's historical studies.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image well; 'habeat' is as printed (grammatically 'habeant').
Catchword at bottom of page is 'dZ', correctly rendered.
